title: Meta readies 'Muse,' its Hatch consumer AI agent, for a September launch to 2 billion users
subtitle: The Information and The Testing Catalog report Meta's Hatch platform — with browser control, persistent cloud environments, and multi-agent tools — will ship as 'Muse' with a premium tier priced up to $199.99/month.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Meta is preparing to launch its consumer AI agent platform — internally called Project Hatch and now confirmed to ship under the production name Muse — as early as this month, according to reporting from The Information, The Testing Catalog, and a September 7 follow-up from Progressive Robot. Muse takes a user goal, decomposes the steps, drives a browser or connected services, and reports back when a multi-step task is done. The distribution surface is the one that matters: Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp, which together reach roughly two billion daily users.

The feature set as described sits at the top end of what shipping consumer agents currently do — /goals-style task specification, persistent cloud environments so a task can resume across sessions, spaces for parallel workstreams, and multi-agent tools that let Muse spawn helper agents inside a single task. Reporting also indicates Meta considered a premium tier priced up to $199.99 per month, which would be the highest sticker for a consumer AI product to date and roughly ten times ChatGPT Plus. Whether that price actually ships or was floated to test elasticity is not yet known.

The strategic frame is that Meta has watched OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google turn agents into the frontier's most-monetized use case, and does not want the next platform-shift to happen inside a competitor's app on its own phones. Hatch/Muse is Meta's attempt to make the agent the app — with Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp as the trust and identity substrate. It is also the first mass-market consumer agent to ship from a company with two billion users, which is a distribution advantage neither OpenAI nor Anthropic can match on day one.

For learners: watch the failure modes, not the features. Consumer agents fail publicly and specifically — a booking made on the wrong dates, an account locked because the agent triggered fraud detection, a purchase made without the user actually confirming. The safety and product work that goes into keeping those failures rare and recoverable is the real engineering, and it is where a company distributing to two billion users has both the largest advantage and the largest liability. When Muse ships, the review to read is not the demo — it is the first post-launch week of complaints.
